title: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC & Beyond
summary: The major design patterns for deciding who can do what, and where a role-based model stops being granular enough. Covers RBAC, ABAC, ACLs, and relationship-based authorization at the level a system design interview expects.

slides.markdown:
[Authentication Fundamentals](authn-fundamentals) opened this group with authentication versus authorization — who you are versus what you're allowed to do. Every topic since has been about the *who*. This topic is entirely about the *what*: the design patterns for modeling permissions at the architecture level, distinct from [Broken Access Control](broken-access-control)'s per-endpoint implementation bugs from the previous group.

The throughline across all of these models is the same tension: **simplicity versus granularity**. A model expressive enough to capture every real permission rule tends to be complex enough that people get it wrong; a model simple enough to reason about tends to hit real cases it can't express cleanly. This topic covers where that tension actually bites, and which model to reach for at which scale.

Every authorization model answers the same question in a different shape: **given an authenticated identity and a requested action on a resource, is it allowed?**

The naive answer — hardcode an `if` statement per feature (`if user.id == 4521: allow`) — breaks down almost immediately: it doesn't scale past a handful of rules, it can't be audited or reasoned about as a whole ("who can currently delete invoices?" has no answer without reading every `if` statement in the codebase), and it can't be changed without a code deploy for something that's fundamentally business policy, not application logic.

Every model in this topic is a structured way to externalize that policy — moving "who can do what" out of scattered conditionals and into a declarative, inspectable, centrally-updatable structure. The models differ in exactly what that structure looks like and how much expressiveness it trades for simplicity.

slides.sectionTitle: RBAC: roles as a bundle of permissions
slides.markdown:
**Role-Based Access Control** groups permissions into named **roles** (`admin`, `editor`, `viewer`), and assigns users to roles rather than to permissions directly. `editor` might bundle "create post," "edit any post," and "delete own post"; a user assigned `editor` gets exactly that bundle.

The payoff is indirection: adding a new permission to what editors can do means updating the `editor` role definition once, and every user with that role picks up the change automatically — no per-user updates needed. Auditing "who can delete posts" is a single lookup of which roles include that permission, then which users hold those roles — a query, not a codebase search.

RBAC is the default starting point for most systems because it maps cleanly onto how organizations already think about access ("she's a manager, managers can approve expenses") and it's simple enough to reason about and audit without specialized tooling.

**Attribute-Based Access Control** evaluates a rule against **attributes** of the user, the resource, and the environment at request time, rather than checking a fixed role assignment: "allow if `user.department == resource.department` AND `time.hour` is between 9 and 17 AND `resource.sensitivity != 'restricted'`."

This is strictly more expressive than RBAC because the decision can depend on **context that changes per request** — the same user gets a different answer at 2am versus 2pm, or accessing a document tagged `restricted` versus one that isn't — without needing a distinct role for every combination of conditions. RBAC would need a combinatorial explosion of roles (`editor-daytime-only`, `editor-restricted-docs`) to express the same policy; ABAC expresses it as one rule referencing attributes directly.

The cost is exactly what you'd expect from more expressiveness: ABAC rules are harder to audit at a glance ("who can access this" requires evaluating the rule against every possible attribute combination, not reading a role list) and harder to reason about when several rules interact.

**Access Control Lists** flip the direction of the other two models: instead of a role or a rule deciding access, each individual **resource** carries its own list of exactly who can do what to it — "this specific document: Alice can edit, Bob can view, everyone else denied."

This is the model behind file system permissions and most "share this document with specific people" features (Google Docs' sharing dialog is an ACL editor). It's the natural fit when permission genuinely varies **per resource instance** rather than following a role pattern — two documents owned by the same user can have completely different, unrelated sharing lists, which RBAC has no clean way to express since roles apply broadly, not per-instance.

The trade-off: ACLs scale permission-management effort with the number of resources, not the number of roles. A system with millions of documents, each individually shared, means millions of independent permission lists to maintain — which is fine when sharing genuinely is per-document, and painful when most resources should actually follow one consistent organizational policy.

The newest major model, popularized by Google's internal **Zanzibar** system (and open-sourced variants like OpenFGA and Ory Keto), models permissions as a **graph of relationships** between users, groups, and resources, then answers authorization questions by traversing that graph: "can Alice view Document X" becomes "is there a path in the relationship graph from Alice to Document X via an `owner`, `editor`, or `viewer` edge, possibly through an intermediate group or folder?"

This generalizes ACLs to handle **inherited and nested** permissions cleanly — "anyone who's a member of the Engineering group can view any document in the Engineering folder" is one relationship rule, not a permission entry duplicated across every document and every group member. Google's own internal use case (answering billions of authorization checks per second across Drive, Docs, and everything else) is the canonical proof this scales to enormous, deeply nested permission graphs.

This is genuinely advanced infrastructure — most systems don't need it, and reaching for it before you have real nested-group-sharing requirements is over-engineering. It's worth recognizing by name for breadth, since it's an increasingly common answer to "how does Google Drive-style sharing actually work" in a system design interview.

![Users connect to roles, and roles connect to permissions, showing that users never connect directly to permissions in RBAC](assets/rbac-indirection.svg)

The diagram's structural point is that indirection layer: users connect to roles, roles connect to permissions, and users never connect to permissions directly. That's exactly what makes RBAC easy to audit and update — change what `editor` bundles once, and every user assigned that role updates automatically, with no per-user edits required.

slides.sectionTitle: RBAC vs ABAC: when roles alone aren't granular enough
slides.markdown:
| | RBAC | ABAC |
|---|---|---|
| **Decision basis** | Fixed role assignment | Rule evaluated against attributes at request time |
| **Context-sensitivity** | None — same role, same permissions, always | Full — can vary by time, location, resource sensitivity, anything modeled as an attribute |
| **Auditability** | High — "who can do X" is a role lookup | Lower — requires evaluating rules against attribute combinations |
| **Granularity ceiling** | Hits a wall when policy needs context RBAC can't express without role explosion | Effectively unbounded, at the cost of rule complexity |
| **Typical scale** | Most business applications | Regulated industries, fine-grained/contextual policy needs |

The honest interview answer to "which is better": start with RBAC, and reach for ABAC specifically when you find yourself creating near-duplicate roles that differ only by a condition (`editor` vs `editor-outside-business-hours`) — that pattern is the concrete signal that role explosion has begun, covered next.

slides.sectionTitle: Role explosion: a role per user defeats the point
slides.markdown:
The failure mode that shows up as RBAC scales past its comfortable range: instead of a handful of shared roles, teams start creating a **new role for every slightly different permission need** — `editor-region-us`, `editor-region-eu`, `editor-no-delete`, eventually approaching one bespoke role per user or team.

Once that happens, RBAC has silently lost its entire advantage: the indirection layer that made "who can do X" a simple role lookup now requires reading dozens of nearly-identical role definitions to find the actual difference, and updating a permission that should apply broadly means editing every one of those near-duplicate roles individually — exactly the maintenance burden RBAC was supposed to eliminate.

The signal to watch for: if you're creating a new role because of a **condition** (region, time, ownership) rather than a genuinely distinct **set of responsibilities**, that's role explosion in progress, and it's the concrete sign to move that condition into an ABAC rule instead of a new role — "editor, but only in their own region" is one attribute check, not a family of regional role variants.

These models answer "what can this identity do within our system." The remaining two topics in this group cover a related but distinct problem: [OAuth 2.0](oauth2) is about delegating limited access to *another* application without sharing a password, and OpenID Connect & SSO builds identity federation on top of that same delegation mechanism — letting one login serve many applications.
